questions.q: A phone sends POST /transfers and gets no response within 30 seconds. What does the phone know about the transfer?
questions.explain: From the client's side, a lost request, a failed request and a succeeded request with a lost response all look the same. That is why retries are necessary, and why the server must make them harmless.
options: It failed, because no response came back
It succeeded, because the request was sent
Nothing: the request may not have arrived, may have failed, or may have succeeded with the response lost
It is still running, so the phone should wait longer

questions.q: Where should a transfer endpoint get the id of the user who is sending money?
questions.explain: Anything in the body is chosen by the caller. The user is whoever the verified credentials say, and then the server checks that this user owns the from account.
options: From a userId field in the JSON body
From the from account, by reading its owner
From the verified session or token on the request
From the Idempotency-Key, which contains the user id

questions.q: Ada asks to send money from account 7, which exists but belongs to Bola. Which answer leaks the least?
questions.explain: If "not yours" and "does not exist" give different answers, anyone can discover which account numbers exist. Answer both the same way.
options: 403 Forbidden: "account 7 is not yours"
404 Not Found: "account 7 was not found", the same as for an account that does not exist
422: "account 7 belongs to Bola Ade"
200 with an empty body

questions.q: What does UPDATE accounts SET balance_kobo = balance_kobo + 1000 WHERE id = 99 do when there is no account 99?
questions.explain: SQL does not treat "no row matched" as an error. Check the number of changed rows (or use RETURNING), or verify the recipient exists before writing.
options: It throws a "row not found" error
It inserts account 99 with a balance of 1000
It succeeds and changes zero rows
It rolls back the current transaction

questions.q: Two transfers of ₦10,000 from an account holding ₦15,000 run at the same time. Each reads the balance, sees ₦15,000, and writes balance - 10000. What is the safe fix?
questions.explain: "Read, decide, write" leaves a gap in which another transfer can act on the same balance. A conditional update closes the gap; the constraint catches any bug that slips through. Idempotency keys solve duplicates, not two different transfers.
options: Read the balance twice before writing
Check the balance in the mobile app before sending
Do the check and the write in one statement: UPDATE … SET balance = balance - $1 WHERE id = $2 AND balance >= $1, plus a CHECK (balance >= 0) constraint
Add an idempotency key to both requests

questions.q: A transfer debits the sender, credits the recipient and inserts a record. Why must all three run in one transaction?
questions.explain: Atomicity: all or nothing. Without it, a failure after the debit leaves the bank with less money than before. A transaction does not help with duplicate requests; that is the idempotency key's job.
options: Transactions make each statement run faster
If any statement fails, all of them are undone, so money never leaves one account without arriving in the other
Transactions stop the same request from arriving twice
PostgreSQL only allows one UPDATE per transaction otherwise

questions.q: When should a mobile app generate the idempotency key for a transfer?
questions.explain: The key names one user intent. A fresh key per attempt makes every retry look new, and one key for all transfers would make the second transfer a replay of the first.
options: Before each HTTP attempt, so every attempt has a fresh key
Once, when the user confirms the transfer, and reuse it for every retry of that transfer
Once per app install, for all transfers
Never; the server generates it and returns it in the response

questions.q: Why are keys stored under (user_id, key) instead of just key?
questions.explain: A stored response may contain balances and account numbers. Scoping keys to the authenticated user means a key only ever replays that user's own responses.
options: To make the index smaller
So one user cannot receive another user's stored response by sending the same key, and users cannot block each other's keys
Because UUIDs are not unique enough on their own
Because PostgreSQL requires composite primary keys for text

questions.q: A client reuses a key from a ₦10,000 transfer for a new ₦50,000 transfer. What should the server do?
questions.explain: Replaying would tell the app a ₦50,000 transfer succeeded when it did not; running it would make keys meaningless. Comparing a stored fingerprint of the request catches the client bug.
options: Replay the ₦10,000 response
Run the ₦50,000 transfer, since it is a different request
Answer 422: the key was already used with a different request
Answer 409 and ask the client to wait

questions.q: Why does the request fingerprint sort object keys before hashing?
questions.explain: A retry may serialize the same object with keys in another order. Without a canonical form, an honest retry would be rejected as a reused key.
options: Sorted JSON is smaller
So {"from":1,"to":2} and {"to":2,"from":1}, the same request, get the same hash
SHA-256 only accepts sorted input
To hide the amount from the database

questions.q: Why must the stored response be written in the same transaction as the transfer?
questions.explain: The work and the record of the work must agree. In one transaction, either both exist or neither does, so a retry either replays or safely redoes.
options: It is faster than two transactions
If the transfer committed but storing the response did not (a crash in between), the next retry would run the transfer again
So the response can include the transaction id
Because jsonb columns can only be written inside a transaction

questions.q: A retry arrives while the first request with the same key is still running. What should the server answer?
questions.explain: The request is identical, so it is not a misuse (422). It is simply too early. A short 409 lets the first request finish; the next retry replays its result.
options: Run the transfer a second time in parallel
Wait forever until the first finishes
409 Conflict (with Retry-After), so the client tries again shortly and then gets the stored result
422, because the key was reused

questions.q: A server claims a key, marks it in progress, and crashes before committing the transfer. Without a lock expiry, what happens?
questions.explain: The key row was committed before the crash, and nothing ever marks it complete. An expiry on the lock lets a later retry take the key over.
options: The next retry runs the transfer normally
Every retry gets 409 forever: the user can never complete that transfer with that key
The database removes the key when the server restarts
The transfer is committed automatically

questions.q: Server A holds a key's lock, becomes very slow, and its lock expires. A retry takes over and completes the transfer. Then server A tries to finish. What stops a second transfer?
questions.explain: A lock expiry alone means two holders can believe they own the key. Tying completion to a token that changes on takeover lets only the current holder commit.
options: Nothing; this case cannot be handled
The CHECK constraint on the balance
The fencing token: completing requires the current lock_id, A's is outdated, so A's transaction rolls back with its transfer
The request fingerprint

questions.q: A transfer is refused with 422 "insufficient funds". The client retries with the same key. What should it get?
questions.explain: Business rejections are real answers. Replaying them keeps the key's meaning simple: one intent, one outcome. Only unexpected errors release the key.
options: The transfer is attempted again, because the balance might have changed
The stored 422 again: it is the final answer to that request; a new attempt after topping up is a new intent with a new key
500, because replaying errors is not allowed
409, because the key is still in use

questions.q: The database is briefly unreachable and the handler throws. What should happen to the idempotency key?
questions.explain: An unexpected error says nothing about the request, and the transaction rolled back, so nothing happened. Replaying a stored 500 would turn a short outage into a permanent failure for that intent.
options: Store the 500 response, so retries replay it
Release it, so a retry can try the transfer again
Keep it in progress until someone deletes it by hand
Mark it completed with an empty body

questions.q: A team stores idempotency keys in a JavaScript Map inside the server. They run three copies behind a load balancer. What goes wrong?
questions.explain: Keys must live where every copy sees them and where they survive restarts: the database, ideally in the same transaction as the work.
options: Nothing, as long as keys are UUIDs
A retry that reaches a different copy (or the same copy after a restart) finds no key and transfers again
The Map becomes too slow after 100 keys
JavaScript Maps cannot store strings as keys

questions.q: Which responses should a transfer client retry, using the same idempotency key?
questions.explain: Retry what might succeed later. A 400 or 422 will fail the same way every time. Thanks to the key, retrying the others can never cause a second transfer.
options: All of them, until it gets a 201
Only 201 and 200
Network errors, 409 "in progress", 429 and 5xx; never 400 or 422
Only network errors; any HTTP response is final

questions.q: Why add random jitter to retry delays?
questions.explain: Without jitter, clients synchronized by one outage stay synchronized, and every retry wave hits at once. Random spreading turns a spike into a gentle slope.
options: To make the delays harder for attackers to predict
So thousands of clients that failed at the same moment do not all retry at the same moment and overload the server again
Because setTimeout is not precise
To make tests non-deterministic

questions.q: Which statement about "exactly-once delivery" is accurate?
questions.explain: To be sure a message arrived, a sender must be willing to send it again, so duplicates are possible. Idempotent processing makes duplicates harmless: effectively once.
options: HTTP/2 guarantees exactly-once delivery
A database transaction guarantees a request is received exactly once
Over an unreliable network you get at-least-once delivery; idempotent processing makes the effect happen once
It is impossible to prevent duplicate effects

questions.q: A transfer must also send an SMS. Where should the SMS be triggered?
questions.explain: Inside the transaction, a later rollback leaves an SMS for a transfer that never happened. After the commit, a crash loses the SMS. The outbox row exists exactly when the transfer does.
options: Inside the transaction, before COMMIT
After COMMIT, in the same request handler
By inserting an outbox row in the same transaction; a worker sends the SMS later, using the row id as its idempotency key
In the mobile app, after it receives the 201

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Two identical requests are two transfers. Nothing in the request says "this is the same one again", which is what an idempotency key adds.

questions.q: The same transfer, now with a key store. What does this print?
questions.explain: The second call finds the key and returns the stored response, marked as a replay, without touching the balances. (A real store lives in the database, not a Map.)

questions.q: The client generates a new key for each attempt. What does this print?
questions.explain: Each retry carries a different key, so the server cannot connect it to the first attempt. The key must be created once per intent and reused.
options: created created 2
created replayed 1
created replayed 2
replayed replayed 0

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: JSON.stringify keeps insertion order, so the two texts differ even though they describe the same request. The canonical form sorts keys, so the fingerprints match.
options:
false true
{"amountKobo":1000000,"from":1,"to":2}

true true
{"amountKobo":1000000,"from":1,"to":2}

false true
{"to":2,"from":1,"amountKobo":1000000}

false false
{"amountKobo":1000000,"from":1,"to":2}

questions.q: This simulates a conditional debit. What does it print?
questions.explain: The check and the change happen together, like UPDATE … WHERE balance >= amount, which returns the number of changed rows. The second debit finds only ₦5,000 and changes nothing; the third fits exactly.

questions.q: A hand-made "transaction" copies the state and restores it on error. What does this print?
questions.explain: The debit happened, then the check failed, and restoring the saved copy undid the debit. A database transaction gives the same all-or-nothing effect, and also protects against crashes.
options:
rolled back: recipient chidi not found
{ ada: 50000, bola: 5000 }

rolled back: recipient chidi not found
{ ada: 40000, bola: 5000 }
{ ada: 40000, bola: 5000, chidi: NaN }

rolled back: recipient chidi not found
{ ada: 40000, bola: 5000, chidi: 10000 }

questions.q: A key was claimed at second 0 with a 30-second lock. What does this print?
questions.explain: Before second 30 the lock is valid. At 31 the retry takes over and sets a new lock until 61, so the retry at 45 is again told to wait.
options: 409 in progress | 409 in progress | take over | 409 in progress
409 in progress | 409 in progress | take over | take over
409 in progress | take over | take over | take over
take over | take over | take over | take over

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: B took the key over, so only B's lock id is current. A finishes late and is refused, so its transaction, and its transfer, roll back.
options:
B: committed
A: lost the lock, roll back

B: committed
A: committed

B: lost the lock, roll back
A: committed

B: lost the lock, roll back
A: lost the lock, roll back

questions.q: What delays (without jitter) does this backoff produce?
questions.explain: Each wait doubles, and a cap stops it from growing without limit: 800 becomes 500. Real clients then add random jitter to each value.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 201 is success, and 422 is a final business answer. The rest may succeed later. "network" >= 500 is false, which is why the string is checked first.
questions.code:
const shouldRetry = (s) => s === "network" || s === 409 || s === 429 || s >= 500;
console.log(["network", 201, 422, 409, 503].filter(shouldRetry));
options: [ 'network', 503 ]

questions.q: Write createKeyStore() returning handle(userId, key, fingerprint, work). A new (userId, key) runs work(), stores and returns its result. The same key and fingerprint returns the stored result with replayed: true. The same key with a different fingerprint returns { status: 422 }. Keys are scoped per user.
questions.explain: The fingerprint check comes before the replay, so a reused key never returns another request's result. User 2's k1 is a different entry. This in-memory version is fine as a test double; in production the store is a database table, written in the same transaction as the work.

questions.q: Write canonical(value) that turns a JSON value into text with object keys sorted at every level (arrays keep their order). Print it for { to: 2, meta: { note: "rent", channel: "app" }, from: 1 }.
questions.explain: Nested objects must be sorted too, or a retry that serializes meta differently gets a different fingerprint. Array order is meaningful data, so it stays.

questions.q: Write checkTransfer({ userId, from, to, amountKobo }, accounts). accounts maps an account id to { owner, status, balance }. Return the first problem as a string, in this order: "invalid_amount" (not a positive safe integer), "same_account", "account_not_found" (missing or not owned by userId), "account_not_active", "recipient_unavailable" (missing or not active), "insufficient_funds"; else "ok".
questions.explain: Every question from the reasoning block becomes one check, done before any money moves. In the database version the balance check is part of the debit itself, so it cannot race with another transfer.

questions.q: Write async function sendWithRetries(send, maxAttempts). It creates one key ("intent-1") before the loop and calls await send(key), which returns a status number or throws for a network error. Retry on a thrown error, 409, 429 or 5xx; return the first other status. Print each attempt as attempt N: …. If all attempts fail, return "unknown".
questions.explain: The key is made once, outside the loop, so every attempt carries the same key and the server can recognise the retries. A real client also waits between attempts, with backoff and jitter.

questions.q: Write begin(row, now, lockMs) for a key row { status, lockedUntil, lockId }. If the status is "completed" return "replay". If the lock is still valid (lockedUntil > now) return "409". Otherwise take over: set a new lockedUntil and a new lockId (use row.lockId + "'") and return "proceed " + lockId.
questions.explain: The takeover changes the lock id, so the original holder can no longer complete: that is the fencing token. In SQL the takeover is one conditional UPDATE … WHERE locked_until < now, so two retries cannot both take over.

questions.q: Make shipping naturally idempotent. Write markShipped(order) for an object { status }: a "paid" order becomes "shipped" and returns "shipped"; an already shipped order returns "already shipped" without error; any other status returns "error: order is <status>". Call it twice on a paid order and once on a cancelled one.
questions.explain: Setting a target state is idempotent: doing it again changes nothing. Reporting the repeat as success, not as an error, lets clients retry freely. Moving money is not like this, which is why transfers need keys.
questions.expected:
shipped
already shipped
error: order is cancelled

questions.q: Write checkInvariant(before, after) that compares two balance objects and prints "ok: total ₦X" when the totals (in kobo) are equal, or "broken: ₦Y went missing" (or "appeared" when positive) when they differ. Amounts are in kobo; print naira with / 100 and toLocaleString("en-NG").
questions.explain: A transfer moves money but never creates or destroys it. Checking that invariant after every test catches partial failures, double debits and lost credits, whatever caused them.
